extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of formal logic and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A didactic exposition on the nature and role of definitions, postulates, and different forms of inference (conversion, induction, ratiocination/syllogism), with guidance on distinguishing genuine reasoning from mere verbal equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions concern names not things
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions are properly of names only, and not of things; a definition states the meaning of a word rather than asserting facts about real objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that treating definitions as premises about things leads to category errors. Example: replace 'is' with 'means' in definitions to avoid illicit existential assumptions. Even when definitions appear to describe objects (e.g., circle), the definitional statement itself only concerns the meaning of the word unless a separate postulate of existence is supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulates (implied existence) are the real premises in demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many demonstrative conclusions commonly thought to follow from definitions actually rest on tacit postulates — assumptions that the corresponding object or idea exists (e.g., the postulate that a circle about centre A with radius BA may be described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations require the postulate that a figure with the specified properties exists; whether this admissibility is grounded in intuition or proof is debatable, but the postulate — not the bare definition — is the premise that supports geometric theorems. Example: the equality of radii follows because the figure has equal radii, and our warrant to assume such a figure is the postulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions cannot serve as existential premises
rubrics_metrics.description: If one uses a definition as though it implied the real existence of the defined thing, one may derive false conclusions when no such thing exists (e.g., the 'dragon' example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dragon syllogism shows that treating definitional clauses as assertions of real existence allows valid syllogisms with true premises to yield false conclusions; the hidden existential assumption must be made explicit (e.g., 'a dragon is a really existing thing...') to avoid this error. To keep conclusions correct, treat definitions as statements about meanings or ideas unless an independent existence postulate is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal (meaning) propositions are not provable facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions respecting the meaning of words (definitions, verbal propositions) are essentially arbitrary and not susceptible to truth or falsity in the way that propositions about things are; they are not subjects for proof or disproof in the same sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes verbal from real propositions: logical or demonstrative proof applies to propositions about facts/phenomena, not to mere stipulations about language. Thus, when analyzing what can be proved, identify whether the proposition concerns meaning (verbal) or facts (real).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real propositions relate to facts, causes, and basic relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Real (non-verbal) propositions have as their real subject facts/phenomena of consciousness or hidden causes/powers, and they assert existence, order in place or time, causation, or resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an analysis of the import of propositions: every proposition asserts that a subject possesses an attribute or that attributes are conjoined. Use this taxonomy to determine what kind of evidence or proof is appropriate for a given claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish apparent (tautological) inferences from real inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Many cases that appear to be inferences are merely restatements or rewordings (equipollency/equivalence) of the same assertion and do not constitute genuine reasoning that produces new truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include simple paraphrase, deriving a particular from a universal (All A is B → Some A is B), or inferring predicates already connoted by prior predicates (Socrates is a man → Socrates is a living creature). These should be recognized and not treated as substantive proofs. Logical training should cultivate skill in detecting identity under varied wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion rules and their limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion (turning predicate into subject and vice versa) is sometimes legitimate but subject to specific constraints: e.g., Some A is B ⇒ Some B is A; All A is B does not imply All B is A but implies Some B is A (conversion per accidens); No A is B ⇒ No B is A; particular negatives have restricted conversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text details permissible conversions and warns that converting universals typically yields only a particular. For particular negatives (Some A is not B) conversion requires contraposition and may change terms (e.g., 'a thing which is not B'). Use the stated conversion forms cautiously and recognize when conversion merely produces an equivalent or a weaker proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction vs Ratiocination (classification of inference types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction infers a conclusion more general than its premises (from particulars to general), whereas Ratiocination (syllogism) infers conclusions equally general or less general than the premises (from generals to particulars or between generals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational definition: if the conclusion is more general than the largest premise, label it induction; if equally or less general, ratiocination. The text notes a third species of reasoning that underlies both and explains the pedagogical order of treating ratiocination before induction in a system aiming to trace derived truths to their grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of meaning via subject-attribute framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful less-abstruse expression for the import of propositions is the subject-attribute analysis: every proposition asserts that a given subject does or does not possess some attribute, or that attributes are or are not conjoined in subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framework is recommended as sufficiently scientific for many logical purposes and helps classify propositions for purposes of proof and inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for defining abstract/general names
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining an abstract name requires examining whether the objects called by the name form a class, whether they have a common attribute, and if not, determining the largest subset that shares a general resemblance; then choose differentiæ that select attributes of greatest importance and lead to the most interesting propria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) investigate usage/convention to see if meaning can be fixed; (2) examine resemblances among objects denoted; (3) ascertain common attributes; (4) if no universal commonality exists, determine a suitable artificial class and confine the name's denotation. Philosophers should prefer differentiæ that yield significant and consequential properties rather than obscure traits. Examples include the difficulty of defining 'justice' or 'virtue'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect spontaneous language growth when remodeling definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Established usage and spontaneous development of language contain practical classifications shaped by long experience and thus should inform philosophical attempts to systematize or redefine terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises that logicians remoulding language should consider customary groupings as valuable evidence: common usage indicates obvious resemblance and historical associations which can be useful materials for systematic definitions. Avoid ignoring the index of real connections that history of usage may reveal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate truth of postulates suffices for demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when postulates are not exactly true in nature (e.g., no perfect circle with exactly equal radii exists), enough of the postulate's truth is present to support the true parts of the conclusion; exact literal truth of postulates is not always required for demonstrative certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses an apparent paradox: geometrical conclusions can be certain even though their postulates are idealizations. The text promises a fuller treatment later (in Demonstration) but asserts that the relevant part of the postulate needed for the conclusion is true in the required sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical training: cultivate recognition of identity under varying language
rubrics_metrics.description: An important objective of logical discipline is the ability to discern rapidly and surely the identity of an assertion when expressed in different words (equipollency, opposition of propositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond formal rules, practice should focus on detecting when conclusions add nothing new and when differences of wording conceal or reveal genuine inferential content. The technical vocabulary (contraries, subcontraries, contradictories, subalterns) serves chiefly to facilitate this cognitive skill.
